title: Bit Manipulation
summary: Numbers are just rows of switches. Flip, read, and combine them directly, and a class of impossible-looking problems collapses into one or two lines — all O(1).

blocks.markdown:
An integer is a fixed row of bits, each worth a power of two — bit manipulation works those switches directly.

- Treat one integer as a **number**, a **set of flags**, or a tiny **boolean array** — whichever helps.
- Five operators: **AND** `&`, **OR** `|`, **XOR** `^`, **NOT** `~`, and **shifts** `<<` `>>`.
- Nearly every trick is **O(1) time, O(1) space** — that is the whole appeal.
- Each operator is a single CPU instruction, about as fast as computation gets.

blocks.subTitle: When to reach for it
blocks.markdown:
Reach for bits when the question is awkward as math but trivial as switches.

| When you want to… | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Test if one bit is on | `x & (1 << i)` |
| Find the unique unpaired number | XOR the whole array |
| Check power of two | `(x & (x-1)) == 0` |
| Represent a small subset | integer bitmask |

blocks.subTitle: Place values & shifts
blocks.markdown:
A bit at position `i` (counting from 0 on the right) contributes `2^i` when it is 1.

- So `1011` is `8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11`.
- Position 0 is the **least significant bit (LSB)**; the highest used bit is the **MSB**.
- **Shift left** `<< 1` slides bits left — multiplies by 2.
- **Shift right** `>> 1` slides right — divides by 2, dropping the remainder.
- `1 << i` builds a mask with only bit `i` set.

blocks.subTitle: The five operators
blocks.markdown:
Each operator acts bit-by-bit and has a typical job.

- **AND `&`** — 1 only if both are 1. Tests and clears (masks off).
- **OR `|`** — 1 if either is 1. Sets bits on.
- **XOR `^`** — 1 if the bits differ. Toggles and cancels pairs.
- **NOT `~`** — flips every bit; equals `-x - 1`.
- Key XOR facts: `a ^ 0 = a`, `a ^ a = 0`, and order doesn't matter (commutative, associative).

blocks.subTitle: Two's complement
blocks.markdown:
To negate a number, flip every bit and add 1 — so `-x == ~x + 1`.

![Two's complement of -5 in three steps](assets/a18-bit-manipulation/twos-complement.svg)

- The top bit falls out as a **sign indicator**: 0 non-negative, 1 negative — not a flag you set by hand.
- The same addition circuit then works for positive and negative numbers, no special cases.
- `5 + (-5)` overflows the 8 bits back to all zeros — exactly what negation means.
- This identity is why `x & -x` isolates the lowest set bit.

assets.alt: Two's complement of -5 in three steps

blocks.subTitle: The four single-bit moves
blocks.markdown:
Build `mask = 1 << i`, then read or change one bit. Each is O(1).

```python
is_set   = (x >> i) & 1      # 1 if bit i is on
set_bit  = x | (1 << i)      # force bit i to 1
clear    = x & ~(1 << i)     # force bit i to 0
toggle   = x ^ (1 << i)      # flip bit i
```

- These compile to one or two CPU instructions and touch a single register.
- AND tests and clears, OR sets, XOR toggles — the operator picks the verb.

blocks.subTitle: The standard one-liners
blocks.markdown:
A handful of idioms cover most bit problems.

```python
lowest_set   = x & -x          # isolate rightmost 1-bit
clear_lowest = x & (x - 1)     # remove rightmost 1-bit
is_pow2      = x > 0 and (x & (x - 1)) == 0
```

- `x & (x-1)` works because `x-1` flips the lowest 1 and fills below it with 1s; AND wipes that region.
- A power of two has exactly **one** set bit, so clearing it gives 0 — that's the test.
- Loop `x &= x-1` and count to get the **population count** (set-bit count).

blocks.subTitle: XOR cancels pairs
blocks.markdown:
Because `a ^ a = 0` and order doesn't matter, XOR-ing a whole array leaves only the odd-one-out.

```python
def find_unique(nums):
    acc = 0
    for v in nums:
        acc ^= v        # pairs cancel to 0
    return acc
```

- Every paired value cancels itself; the lone element survives.
- **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space — beats the hash-set version's O(n) space ([a03-hashing](a03-hashing.md)).

blocks.subTitle: An integer as a set
blocks.markdown:
Store any subset of ~30–60 items in one integer: bit `i` on means item `i` is in the set.

![Integer storing the subset apple and milk as binary 0011](assets/a18-bit-manipulation/bitmask-subset.svg)

- **Add** `mask | (1 << i)`, **remove** `mask & ~(1 << i)`, **test** `(mask >> i) & 1`.
- **Union** `a | b`, **intersection** `a & b`, **difference** `a & ~b` — all O(1).
- Empty set is `0`; full set of `n` is `(1 << n) - 1`.
- This is the foundation of **bitmask DP** ([a15-dynamic-programming-2](a15-dynamic-programming-2.md)).

assets.alt: Integer storing the subset apple and milk as binary 0011

blocks.markdown:
Bit tricks are compact and fast but can be cryptic — weigh the win.

- **Clarity vs. speed** — use well-known idioms where the win is real, and comment them.
- **Capacity** — a bitmask holds only as many items as the integer has bits (32 or 64); beyond that, use a bitset.
- **Premature optimization** — the compiler already turns `x * 2` into a shift; reach for bits for *expressiveness* (flags, sets, masks), not blind speed.
- **Heuristic** — small fixed flags or `n ≤ 20` subset enumeration → bitmask; large or subtle logic → plain set.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
Bit packing runs the systems you use daily.

- **Unix permissions** — `rwx` for owner/group/other as nine bits (octal `0755`); checking write access is one AND.
- **Kernel event flags** — `epoll`/`poll` events OR-ed into one integer; the kernel ANDs to test them. TCP `SYN`/`ACK`/`FIN` are packed bits too.
- **Bloom filters** — giant bit arrays in Cassandra and caches; add sets bits, query tests them ([b05-caching](b05-caching.md)).
- **Redis bitmaps** — one bit per user; a billion users fit in 125 MB, answered by population count.

blocks.subTitle: Signals in production
blocks.markdown:
Bit logic rarely has a dashboard, but it breaks in measurable ways.

- **Off-by-one bit positions** after adding or reordering a flag — silently grants or revokes access; assert masks in tests.
- **Negative IDs or weird sort orders** — a high bit got set unexpectedly; suspect integer overflow.
- **Rising Bloom-filter false positives** — the bit array is too full; shows up as extra disk reads.
- **popcount hotspots** — in analytics, population counting can dominate CPU; use the hardware instruction.

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **Operator precedence.** In C-family languages `&` `|` `^` bind looser than `==`, so `x & 1 == 0` is wrong — write `(x & 1) == 0`.
- **Shifting too far.** Shifting a 32-bit value by ≥ 32 is undefined or wraps; keep shifts within the width.
- **`1 << i` overflow.** `1 << 40` overflows a 32-bit int — use a 64-bit literal `1L << 40`.
- **Signed vs. logical shift.** `>>` may sign-extend; Java adds `>>>` for zero-fill. Know which you use.
- **Bitmask truncation.** More items than bits, and the top bits silently fall off.
